title: "Sarah's Slide Template"
subtitle: "Reusable clean-revealjs starting point + formatting reference"
author:
  - name: Dr. Sarah Dreier
    affiliation: University of New Mexico
format:
  clean-revealjs:
    self-contained: true
    slide-number: true
    footer: "POLS 2140 — Intro to Political Analysis"
    # Emphasis shortcut: write  [text]{.hl}  anywhere for teal-bold emphasis
    # (the deck's standard highlight — same as "emphasize" = teal).
    include-in-header:
      text: |
        <style>.reveal .hl { color: #107895 !important; font-weight: 700; }</style>
    # Every external link opens in a new tab automatically, so a plain
    # [text](https://…) is all you ever write for a hyperlink — no {target="_blank"},
    # no raw <a> tag.
    include-after-body:
      text: |
        <script>
          document.querySelectorAll('a[href^="http"]').forEach(function (a) {
            a.target = "_blank"; a.rel = "noopener";
          });
        </script>

# Bibliography in APA format. Keep these two lines in every deck; do NOT add
# `biblio-title:` (it collides with the manual `## References` slide below and
# suppresses that slide's heading). CSL style from https://github.com/citation-style-language/styles

bibliography: references_2140.bib
csl: apa.csl

## How to use this file

Duplicate this file to start a new deck, delete the slides you don't need, and build from the examples below. Everything here uses `format: clean-revealjs` — no custom `.css` file, no manual spacer `<div>`s, no visibility hacks. The theme handles spacing/centering on its own.

To publish: `quarto render your_file.qmd`

**Every deck should open with two blank slides, in this order** — Reading Prompt, then Announcements (see above; no "Wrap up from last class" slide) — and **end with a TL;DR slide, then a References slide** (see the last two slides in this file) summarizing that lecture's 3–5 main takeaways and citing anything referenced. Fill in the two opening slides and generate real takeaway content for the closing slide once the deck has actual lecture content — they're intentionally blank/placeholder here since this is just the template.

---

## Pausing between lines or images {.smaller}

**The simplest way — three dots on their own line:**

```
Line one shows immediately.

. . .

Line two waits for a click.

. . .

An image can pause too — same trick, no wrapping needed.

![](my_image.png)
```

Just type `. . .` (three dots, spaces between them) on its own blank-line-separated line, in **plain slide markdown** — no `:::` wrapper, no HTML needed. Everything after it becomes a click-to-reveal fragment; add another `. . .` for another pause.

This is a real, working feature — implemented by `_extensions/grantmcdermott/clean/pause-dots.lua`, a filter registered on this theme that every deck using `clean-revealjs` picks up automatically. It works inside plain slide markdown, inside Pandoc `::: {...}` fenced divs, and inside `layout=` panel columns.

**One situation where it still doesn't work — use `.fragment` instead:**

- **Inside a raw HTML `<div>...</div>` block** (e.g. `<div class="text-center">`). The filter deliberately leaves `. . .` alone there and prints a build-time warning, rather than risk producing malformed nested HTML by wrapping across the raw div's own open/close tags. Wrap the content in a fragment div instead:
  ```
  <div class="fragment">
  This pauses correctly inside HTML.
  </div>
  ```

**One thing to know about lists:** `. . .` between items in the same bullet list still splits it into two separate `<ul>` elements (a Pandoc markdown-parsing quirk, not something the filter can avoid) — it works as a pause, but for a single continuous list it's cleaner to wrap the whole thing in `.incremental` instead so every item pauses on its own click without splitting the underlying HTML:
   ```
   ::: {.incremental}
   - First point
   - Second point
   - Third point
   :::
   ```

## Default: pause between bullets and lines

Unless a slide is meant to dump everything at once (e.g. a dense links/resources slide), **default to pausing between bullets and between separate lines/sentences** so the presenter reveals one idea at a time:

- **Bullet lists (`-`/`1.`):** wrap the whole list in `::: {.incremental}` so every item is its own click — this works even nested inside a raw HTML `<div>` (Pandoc still parses list markdown inside HTML blocks).
- **Separate lines/paragraphs that aren't a list:** a plain `. . .` between them now works reliably (see "Pausing between lines or images" above) — including inside `::: {...}` fenced divs and `layout=` columns. The one place it still doesn't work is inside a raw HTML `<div>...</div>` block; use `::: {.fragment}` there instead, and don't share one fragment wrapper across multiple lines you want to reveal separately — each line needs its own `.fragment` (or its own `. . .` marker).
- A slide with just one short idea, or one meant to be read as a whole (links/resources, a single quote), doesn't need this — use judgment.

## Two-column layout via `layout=` (more control) {.smaller}

`.columns`/`.column` above is the simplest option. For exact proportional control (and to combine with images/captions/notes cleanly), use a `layout=` panel instead:

```
:::: {layout="[42,58]"}

::: {#first-column}
<div style="font-size: 0.9em; line-height: 1.3;">
Text column content here.
</div>
:::

::: {#second-column}
<div style="text-align: center;">
![](my_image.png){style="max-height: 40vh; width: auto;"}
</div>
:::

::::
```

The numbers are relative proportions (don't need to sum to 100). **Put custom `style` on a nested `<div>` inside each column** — not on `#first-column`/`#second-column` itself — see the gotcha further down; Quarto silently discards it otherwise.

---

## Grid layout: multi-row panels & grouped pauses {.smaller}

For more than two columns, or extra full-width rows, use `.grid`/`.grid-item` instead of a `layout=` panel:

```
:::: {.grid layout="[1,2]"}
::: {.grid-item}
Text here.
:::
::: {.grid-item}
![](chart.png)
:::
::::

:::: {.grid}
::: {.grid-item span-col=2}
A full-width row below the two columns above.
:::
::::
```

`span-col=N` makes one grid item span N columns — handy for a full-width row under a multi-column row.

**Grouping multiple elements to reveal on the same click:** give each element the same `fragment-index`:

```
::: {.grid-item .fragment fragment-index=1 .fade-in}
Text that appears on click 1.
:::

::: {.grid-item .fragment fragment-index=1 .fade-in}
![](chart.png)
:::
```

Both fade in together on that first click; use `fragment-index=2` on the next group for a second, separate click.

Use `{background-color="#1a1a1a"}` on the slide heading (even an empty one) for a full-bleed dark slide, and set text color inline since the theme's default text is dark:

```

<div style="color:#ffffff;">
Your content here.
</div>
```

# A section divider slide {background-color="#2c3e50"}

A single `#` heading (instead of `##`) makes a full-bleed section-break slide — handy for splitting a lecture into parts. **Rule: always put `{background-color="#2c3e50"}` on it** — that slate is the standard contrast color for these decks, and the theme flips the heading text to light automatically. A bare `#` divider with no background color is an omission to fix, not a style choice.

If the divider slide also carries body text (a few prompt questions, say), wrap that content in `::: {style="color: #ffffff;"}` — the theme only lightens the heading, not the body, so unwrapped paragraphs render dark-on-slate.

## Gotcha: blockquotes nested under a bullet

If you want a note/blockquote to appear under a specific bullet (not as a new top-level block), you need a **blank line** before the `>` — otherwise Pandoc doesn't parse it as a real blockquote and it renders as broken literal text.

```
- My bullet point

  > A properly nested note under that bullet.
```

---

## Gotcha: image paths

Always double-check the image path is relative to *this* file's location, not to the folder in general. A quick `quarto render` will silently produce a blank spot (or a console warning) if the path is wrong — check the rendered `.html` if an image doesn't show up.

## Hyperlinks (text)

Just use Markdown: `[link text](https://the-url.com)`. The `include-after-body` script in this
file's YAML gives every external link `target="_blank"` at load time, so links open in a new tab
without losing the slide — you never need `{target="_blank"}` or a hand-written `<a>` tag.

Emphasis shortcut (also from the YAML): `[text]{.hl}` renders teal-bold — the deck's standard
highlight.

## Linking an image

Wrap the `<img>` in a plain `<a>` tag (the after-body script tabs it out too):

```
<a href="https://example.com/">
<img src="my_image.png" style="width: 100%;" />
</a>
```

---

## Gotcha: `class="fragment"` directly on an `<img>` tag gets silently dropped {.smaller}

With `self-contained: true`, Quarto re-embeds every image as a base64 `data:` URI — and when it rebuilds the `<img>` tag to do that, it only keeps `src`/`alt`/`style`-type attributes and **drops a `class="fragment"` written directly on the tag**, with no warning. The image just never pauses.

```
<!-- Doesn't work — class gets stripped during self-contained image embedding -->
<img src="my_image.png" class="fragment" style="width: 100%;" />

<!-- Works — wrap it in a fragment div instead -->
::: {.fragment}
<img src="my_image.png" style="width: 100%;" />
:::
```

Same underlying lesson as the `layout=` panel gotcha above: **verify by grepping the rendered `.html`, not the `.qmd`** — since the image's filename disappears into the base64 blob, search for the wrapping `class="fragment"` div instead of the image's `src`.

---

## Gotcha: shrinking a dense slide

If a slide has too much content, add `{.smaller}` right after the heading text — no custom CSS class needed, it's built into the theme:

```
## A dense slide {.smaller}
```

If that's not enough (e.g. a `layout=` panel or raw HTML block `{.smaller}` doesn't reach), see "Fitting content to the slide" below.

---

## Gotcha: `layout=` columns silently drop custom styles {.smaller}

`:::: {layout="[X,Y]"}` column panels are convenient, but Quarto **overwrites the `style` attribute** on `::: {#first-column style="..."}` / `#second-column` with its own auto-generated `flex-basis` rule — any custom `font-size`, `line-height`, `display: flex`, etc. placed directly on that column div is silently discarded at render time. There's no warning; the `.qmd` looks correct and `quarto render` succeeds anyway.

**Fix:** put your styling on a nested `<div>` *inside* the column instead of on the column div itself:

```
::: {#first-column}
<div style="font-size: 0.9em; line-height: 1.3;">
Your content here.
</div>
:::
```

**Always verify a style change actually landed** — grep the rendered `.html` for it after `quarto render`; don't just trust that editing the `.qmd` was enough.

---

## Fitting content to the slide (without going comically small) {.smaller}

**Base rule: if a slide's text overflows the screen, set it to `font-size: 0.9em` first.** Apply it as `## Slide Title {style="font-size: 0.9em;"}` on the heading — that puts the `style` on the generated `<section>`, so it scales the whole slide with one clean mechanism. This is the default first move, not a last resort.

1. **0.9em via the heading `style=` attribute is step one.** Don't reach for `{.smaller}` as the default fix — it's a bigger, less predictable jump (the theme's own preset reduction) than a controlled 0.9em.
2. **Never stack `{.smaller}` and an explicit `font-size` on the same slide.** They compound (e.g. `.smaller`'s own reduction × 0.9 again) and overshoot into unreadably tiny — this has actually happened. Pick one mechanism per slide.
3. **If 0.9em alone doesn't clear the overflow**, then: check column proportions — a narrow `layout="[25,75]"` text column forces long bullets to wrap into many lines, and rebalancing (e.g. `[42,58]`) is often the real fix, not more shrinking.
4. **Cap images by `max-height` in `vh` units** (e.g. `style="max-height: 40vh; width: auto;"`), not just `width: 100%` — width-only sizing lets a tall image blow past the slide regardless of column width.
5. **Tighten margins/line-height before dropping font-size further.** Cutting `line-height` (to ~1.2–1.3) and list-item `margin-bottom` (to ~0.15–0.2em) often recovers enough room without going below 0.9em at all.
6. **Only drop below 0.9em if 1–5 didn't create enough room**, and treat that as unusual — technically-not-overflowing-but-uncomfortably-tiny isn't a fix.
7. **Default toward bigger, not smaller.** Once content fits, images and text should be as large as the slide comfortably allows — keep normal margins/column gaps rather than cramming just because there's room to shrink more.
8. **Always render and check.** `quarto render`, then actually look at (or grep) the output — don't assume a style change worked, especially inside a `layout=` column panel (see the gotcha above).

## Citing sources — always use `@key` citations, never hand-written links {.smaller}

**Every source citation on a slide uses a Quarto `@key` citation** keyed to an entry in `references_2140.bib`. Do **not** hand-write `<a href>` links or plain-text "(Author Year)" strings for sources — `@key` renders a clickable citation that jumps to the References slide, and citeproc formats the full APA entry there automatically.

- Parenthetical: `[@dignazio2020data]` → "(D'Ignazio & Klein, 2020)"
- Narrative: `@dignazio2020data` → "D'Ignazio & Klein (2020)"
- With a locator: `@silberzahn2018many [Fig. 2, p. 346]` → "Silberzahn et al. (2018, Fig. 2, p. 346)"
- As a source line under a figure: put it in a fenced div so citeproc processes it — `::: {style="font-size: 0.6em; color: #666;"}` / `Source: @silberzahn2018many [p. 345]` / `:::`. (A raw HTML `<div>` swallows the citation — use `:::`, not `<div>`.)

If the source isn't in `references_2140.bib` yet, add a BibTeX entry for it there first.

## For [Day]:

**Every deck's last three slides, in this order: next-class reading, TL;DR, References.** This slide is the first of those three — it names the *next* class meeting's assigned reading, using the `## For [Day]:` heading style (matches the "For Thursday:" / "For Tuesday:" pattern already used elsewhere in this course's decks). Pull the actual reading from the syllabus's Course Schedule, verified against it, not invented:

<a href="https://skdreier.github.io/POLS2140/" target="_blank">*Fundamentals*, Ch. X — see the full schedule on the syllabus</a>

---

## TL;DR

**Second-to-last slide.** Once the deck has real lecture content, replace this with 3–5 genuine main takeaways generated from *that lecture's* actual material — not generic placeholders. Example shape:

- Point one — the single biggest idea from the lecture
- Point two — a key term/concept students should walk away knowing
- Point three — how this connects to the next class or an assignment
- (Point four/five if the lecture genuinely covered that much ground — don't pad to hit 5)

---

## References {.smaller}

::: {#refs}
:::

**Every deck ends with this slide, even with nothing yet cited.** Without a `bibliography:` set, or without this `::: {#refs}` placeholder, Quarto tacks the reference list onto whatever the last content slide is and it overflows. The `## References` heading only renders if nothing (e.g. an HTML comment block) sits between it and the `::: {#refs}` div, and if `biblio-title:` is NOT set in the YAML.
